Messages.Author: Brian
Messages.Body:
Syllogism for Your Pleasure:

1. If something is punished, that thing is known of.
2. If something is known of, is not secret.
3. If something is not secret, it is not collusion.
Therefore
4. If something is punished, it is not collusion.

Of course, something known about by only the colluders and, say, one
judge is still relatively "secret"...that and people are punished for
/having/ colluded, not while colluding. Still, I thought it was cute.

Also, this from Dr. Albert Merhabian's "Silent Messages":

Communication is 7% words, 53% body language, and 40% tone of voice.

If this is true, then approximately 93% of collusion is unstated, but
understood. I don't think you can regulate body language or tone of
voice at a tournament, and I'd just rather you not try.

My friend Aaron and I aren't deal breakers. WE both know it. We may
make a deal with the other without fear of it being broken.

This may not sound like much, but this gives us an advantage against
other players who don't know us. If two players offer me similar
deals, I'll go with Aaron over the other, just because I know he'll
keep his end--which benefits myself (security) and Aaron at the
expense of the others at the table.

Recently joining the Seattle playgroup has shown me just HOW MUCH this
sort of thing can matter. Being an outsider, I really have no idea
who these people are or how they play. I think that knowledge does
give them a significant edge over myself--and in a way, it qualifies
as collusion.

Perhaps what people are talking about on the "collusion" post is not
collusion, but spite/lack of interest/frustration/bad decision making.
In the finals last night, it was down to

myself (pool about 7, controlled 6 Tremere/!Tremere),
my prey Fletcher (pool about 8, just Beast)
and his prey/my pred Scott (bout 20 pool, 6 pot weenies).

Scott used the Succubus Club to give Fletcher pool to Beast all over
me...never mind that if I die before Scott, Fletcher can't win (Scott
and I had each a VP to Fletcher's 0), or that I was willing to back
off to have him work on our common enemy Scott...he took the bait, I
was rushed from both sides, and I ran out of cards...not before
killing Fletcher, though. (I'm sure neither one of us are happy with
that.)

Could I accuse Fletcher of collusion? No. I have no idea what cards
were in his hand or what he thought my deck capable of (or Scott's, or
his own.) I just know that it sucked, is all. It looked to me like
he was basically screwed either way and had to decide which way to
roll over, but even if my offer was reasonable, reason is not a
prerequisite to playing this game. You can't expect everyone who
plays to play to win, or to play well, or even to have played before.
That's what anti-collusion rules amount to, really, and players are
not and never will be that predictable.

Though you can increase it with incentives (like enforcing tournament
points.)

--Brian

and you'll get the table win with 3VP." That way, Fletcher would have gotten

Of course you can! Jeez! This is one of the statements that pops up every so
often, and I'll refute it every time I see it:

Since, by definition, a game with victory conditions MUST be played to win, you
SHOULD expect players to play to win.

Why would you ever again play with a player that doesn't play to win? I

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On 25 Apr 2002 15:57:54 -0700, Brian wrote:

>Syllogism for Your Pleasure:
>
>1. If something is punished, that thing is known of.
>2. If something is known of, is not secret.
>3. If something is not secret, it is not collusion.
>Therefore
>4. If something is punished, it is not collusion.

Secrecy is not an essential ingredient of collusion. Lasombra's
dictionary definition is inadequate. Here's one from a bigger
dictionary (Chambers):

"collude, v.i. to play into each other's hands: to act in concert,
esp. in a fraud. ns. colluder; collusion the act of colluding: a
secret agreement to deceive, esp. one made bteween the opposing
parties in a lawsuit: deceit ... [L. colludere, collusum, from col-
and ludere, to play.]"

The essential idea is that parties who ought to be playing against
each other or independently are instead playing together. Such
arrangements tend to be kept secret because they are illicit and so
will, as you say, be punished or undone if discovered. But you cannot
escape these consequences by being open about it. If two or more VTES
players announce at the outset that they are playing as partners or as
a team then they would still be guilty of collusion.

Andrew

Andrew S. Davidson <a...@csi.com> wrote in message news:<FC6EED2BBC402682.BD2E76C3...@lp.airnews.net>...


We had an occurence at a recent tournament. Weenine Pre/Vote (already
ousted S&B) bleeding into Arhimane intercept into Bruise and
Bleed(already ousted toreador). So,

Weenie vote
Arhimane Intercept
Bruise and Bleed

The weenies made deal with arhimanes....don't block me and I will not
call any damaging votes against you. Now the strategy was to get a lot
of weenines out and kill the big bleed predator who quickly. The
Arhimanes agreed, I can only think that they did not want the bleed
deck to sweep and pounced on an opportunity for a VP. As it turns out,
the weenies did oust the Bruise and bleed for the ahrimanes and then
finished the Arhimanes off to take the day.

Is this a case of collusion? The weenines made the deal with victory
in mind, it may seem a peculiar strategy to some (and not to others),
but does the fact that they were not chasing maximum VP's (but still
overall victory) have any relevance? The bruise and bleed raised the
question of collusion during the course of the game, but it was never
really an open accusation and seemed to not be taken all that
seriously. I would be interested to hear any comments on this, as well
as any other similar occurences.
-scrote

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
scrote wrote:
> but does the fact that they were not chasing maximum VP's (but still
> overall victory) have any relevance?

No.

As a refressher (restating the position again - Lasombra, perhaps this
is ready for the FAQ?):

Players must play to win. If one has multiple paths to victory, then
one is free to choose from among those paths.

If one cannot win, then one is obliged to maximize one's VPs. If there
are multiple paths available to achieve the most VPs one can get,
then one is free to choose.

If one cannot win, and the most VPs one can acquire is "0 more
than currently acquired", then one is free to acquire those 0
more VPs in any manner one wishes.

--

Messages.Body:
On 26 Apr 2002 06:11:02 -0700, scrote wrote:

>The weenies made deal with arhimanes....don't block me and I will not
>call any damaging votes against you. Now the strategy was to get a lot
>of weenines out and kill the big bleed predator who quickly. The
>Arhimanes agreed, I can only think that they did not want the bleed
>deck to sweep and pounced on an opportunity for a VP. As it turns out,
>the weenies did oust the Bruise and bleed for the ahrimanes and then
>finished the Arhimanes off to take the day.

What sort of votes were these? The usual Kine Resources Contested
damages two players and it's not clear how the weenie deck shares out
the damage in this situation.

Tactical details aside, you can get a loop in this triangular
situation. With both prey and predator combining against him, the
bleed deck might offer to better the deal that the Ahrimanes are
getting in your scenario - the bleed deck gets 1 VP and the Ahrimanes
get 2 VP. The weenie deck might then offer a different split to the
bleed deck - the bleed deck gets 2 VP and the weenies get 1 VP. After
each deal is proposed, the player who is being cut out of it can offer
to improve the position of the player who is getting the 1 VP slice so
that he gets 2 VP instead. The players contemplating each new
arrangement always improve their position and so are bound by the
rules to do so. Assuming that everyone is capable of delivering on
any of these 2:1 arrangements, the game then stalemates in an endless
round of negotiation.

If the situation is symmetrical in this way then a resolution of the
impasse is likely to be based on out-of-game factors and so would be
collusive. As the time limit approaches, the players will then have
to agree on a withdrawal deal that gives them all 1 VP each.

My conclusion is that deal-making sucks and the game would be better
without it. And, of course, it should be without it as the rules do
not permit it.

Andrew

Constantly arguing over the definition of collusion isn't constructive. For
one thing, it's quite possible to do things that produce the same results of
collusion without being under V:TES's definition of collusion. Arguing over
whether it is or isn't collusion distracts from the fact that it's just as bad

should definitely have taken the deal since his predator was agreeing to help

What about this scenario then. Different tourney,

!Tremere
!Brujah Rush
Same weenie deck
Bloat deck
Toreador

Before even first turn had elapsed for every player the !Tremere
player said to the !Brujah player that he would not do a single thing
to him until the weenines was ousted (or at least under control). He
even went as far as flicking all his bleeds across the his prey to the
weenines (as the game progressed). No collusion call was made, but
surely this kind of behaviour counts as collusion?

It is a strange example in that it is only really collusion on the
behalf of one party. The !Brujah were obviously happy yo have no
pressure and continue to try and oust their prey, but as for the
!Tremere...was he paying to win, or simply playing to stop a deck that
he didn't like?

I wonder how your path to victory scheme fits into all this? There
existed a *potential* for the weenines to sweep the table without this
kind of deal being made, so it could be construed that the !tremere
were in fact trying to create a potential for more VP's. However, to
so blatantly make a deal before any threat had even been established?

It could also be argued that every deck exists with a *potetial* to
sweep a table. So is it a judgement call or was it collusion?

As it turns out the weenines were ousted with no VP's the !Brujah took
the table and funnily enough, the !Tremere also took no VP's and fifth
place..the weenies got fourth, poetic justice?
-Scrote

The tactical details cannot be set aside, as Scrote suggests. However,
even if they could, think of the deal like this: My predator is
offering to help oust my prey. If I accept this offer I am nearly
guaranteed 1 VP, with the possibility of three if I then proceed to
oust my predator. My prey can offer me a potential 3 VP ONLY by taking
himself out of the game before my predator leaves. This does not mean
that I must accept my predator's deal, since I MUST take tactical
considerations into effect, but the game CANNOT stalemate in
negotiations if only the number of VP offered is taken into account.

Once the tactical details are brought back into it, things change. The
Ahrimanes player could have decided to try to weaken both his predator
and prey, by blocking votes and bleeding simultaneously, but a look at
the board and the hand can give him a rough estimate of the
feasibility of that move. The Ahrimanes probably had either little to
damage his prey with or little intercept left in his hand, possibly
both. Or possibly he simply preferred his options in one-on-one vs a
weenie vote. Either way, he gained one VP, but ultimately lost.

> My conclusion is that deal-making sucks and the game would be better
> without it. And, of course, it should be without it as the rules do
> not permit it.

The rules do not enforce it. There is no rule prohibiting it, either.
There is also no rule allowing me to speak to my opponents, keep my
eyes open during the game, scratch my head, or scratch my butt. This
doesn't mean I want to go through a game without them.

It is a dimension to the game which has few boundaries. A deal, by its
nature, means an exchange, and so it nearly always entails a risk -
much like the rest of the risk. Personally, I rarely accept deals
offered by other players unless I have no clear alternative, but
others are not so careful. It doesn't really matter, since no one is
allowed to make a deal which will keep them from winning unless they
have no chance of winning anyway, which sort of limits the kinds of
deals they could make.

Lactamaeon

Messages.Author: The Lasombra
Messages.Body:
"Brian" asked:

> > If one cannot win, then one is obliged to maximize one's VPs. If there
> > are multiple paths available to achieve the most VPs one can get,
> > then one is free to choose.

> Q: If one cannot win, then one is obliged to maximize one's VPs. If
> there are multiple paths available to achieve the most VPs one can
> get, and one does not recognize any of those paths, what happens?

Then the player does not have the skill to take the VPs,
and they are not truly available to him. You cannot
legislate against poor play / stupid play.

> 1. Must a judge intervene?

A judge must not intervene.

> 2. May a judge intervene?

No.

Carpe noctem.
